Well if we are speaking of a unassembled kit then yes, A rtf is very easy to fly.like this

They come with a basic autopilot already installed that translates your inputs into either an specific attitude, or pitch and roll speeds. Without it, you would be controlling the pitch and roll acceleration (not speed) directly, and when you let go of the stick, it would just keep rotating; same if it bumped on stuff, or was hit my some asymmetric gust of wind or turbulence.

Did some reading on quadcopters "Drones" and most if not all have gyro's, This is built in stabilization. Yes anyone can put a Gyro in any RC aircraft and this is what makes them fly so easy, I have only tried a gyro in mu trex 700 and quickly removed it. I like flying oldschool.

AFAIK, they all have 6 axes "gyros" (accelerometer + gyrometer), they not only can tell how fast they're rotating, but also which way is down; so you can tell it to tilt 15 degrees forward and it will automatically do it, regardless of wind and center of mass (to the limits of it's motors and stuff, of course), without you having to make constant adjustments; and you can let go of the stick and it will stay hovering flat, automatically fighting external forces. (some models got a "rate" mode, where you can control the speed of rotation with the sticks; more advanced than just controlling the acceleration of the rotations)

More expensive ones also got an electronic compass as well (which is usually just considered part of the "gyro" in most descriptions, calling it a "9 axes gyro").

What people are up in arms about are quadcopters. They're the easiest to fly, most stable basic configuration, and there is no longer a skill barrier between anybody who wants to use one for nefarious purposes and it.

Quads are actually just about the least stable, which is why that's practically synonymous with "drone" to the general public. They're theoretically very simple, but most human pilots can't reliably control them without at least a little help from an on-board computer smoothing the flight out a little.

That's why the really suddenly exploded onto the scene when we developed tiny, cheap computers with tiny, cheap accelerometers and rate gyros.

Four points of thrust is the most stable, simplest configurating utilizing the least amount of points, it's a sweet spot. That's why quadcopters are popular and common instead of tricopters or hexacopters (not saying hexacopters don't exist, quadcopters simply outnumber them vastly)

If the points were solid, yes. If it was resting on four legs on the ground, it would be nice.

That is not how aircraft stability works.

EDIT: Specifically, what you need is some way that a disturbance in the attitude of the craft causes a torque that corrects that disturbance. Airplanes have it. Conventional helicopters have it. Quads do not have it unless they're under active electronic control.

I really don't see a point in arguing if you're fighting not to see that four points of thrust makes for the most stability using the simplest mechanical design. It's why they're so popularly commercially available and the dominant design for fixed rotor RC aircraft. The fact that they take a computer input is irrelevant to the fact that they're what people are upset about.

edit: quadcopters counter-rotate, there is no anomalous force that can't be corrected by hand if it has any manifested effect on flight at all. If your motors are properly counteracting then there is no problem. The only computer that needs to be between you and the device input is the microcontroller that interprets inputs into the various rate adjustments at the props.
If there is even a slight asymmetry on the wind, or they bump into something or whatever, it will keep rolling, there is nothing keeping it oriented other than the actions of the onboard electronics.

Term drone for remote control aircraft was coined around the same time as RC. By definition they mean the same thing but you'll get some strong opinions from the RC community when asked.

On one side, an RC plane is flown line of sight and a drone is controlled via video. Which makes sense until you consider the FPV craze. I just built a quad and have every intent of putting a camera on it to use w/ a set of goggles but currently have neither. Is it an RC copter now, but a drone when I upgrade? Seems silly.

Other side is simpler...Drones are military hardware that spy on or kill people. RC airplanes/copters are what the hobbyists fly. It is the least confusing of either definition.

I fall into the latter camp, but given that the US military started deploying their drones around the same time as the semi-autonomous, GPS controlled, iPhone linked, any idiot can turn on and fly for $400 RC quadcopters the terms are entirely interchangeable right now.

To your other point about people being up in arms, given how many idiots are buying these without a lick of common sense as to when and where to fly, the concern is justifiable. Before, the hobby took time and effort to even become moderately proficient. That would weed out the idiots. Don't have that now and it just may end up ruining the sport once politicians inevitably get involved.
Multicopters have the ability to fly in constrained spaces. That's why they are so popular, and why they can get people in trouble for flying where they shouldn't.

Drones can fly semi autonomously or fully autonomously. Drones can keep themselves hovering in one place. Drones can be sent to way points marked on a map in some cases. Drones can be called back to the controller. Although for some reason people are referring to any quad- or hexcopter as a drone. There's an important distinction. A drone may not have anyone flying it at the moment, it may be hovering in the air waiting for instructions. A quadcopter is always being flown by someone, or it's going to crash soon. And while most civilian drones are quadcopters, not all quadcopters are drones.

It is all about the lowered cost and availability. Prior to LiPo battery tech and advanced controllers, Choppers and Quadrachoppers had a steep learning curve and if you wanted to haul decent camera equipment, you had to use gas/nitro choppers - this made them expensive and loud (relatively). Today a person can send $40-50 and get an RTF quad chopper with camera on Amazon. This means its become very easy for anyone to just launch video cameras in the air often inappropriately.

I recall using GWS Slow Sticks with brushless motoros and NiMH and early digital cameras duck taped to record back in the early 2000s. Recording video prior to 2000 was relegated to larger gas powered RC planes with tape based cameras - those operated on 72Mhz and had definite range issues in cities (and just in general - you had chipped frequencies you had to have chip boards to ensure you didnt overlap). Todays craft operate on secure 2.4Ghz so you can fly in cities.

Most importantly rc planes were restricted to altitudes/ranges where the pilot could still see them, where some drones can operate beyond this line of sight, or in abstentia of pilot altogether, meaning there's no guy with a huge antenna standing in plain sight whose responsible and accessible if the craft violates/hurts anybody.

Quads and similar are inherently unstable. Even the most basic ones need a minimal "autopilot" filtering your inputs and adding it's own to keep them flying.

Personally, I think that's enough autonomy/intelligence to justify the name. But I try to not refer to them as such 'cause I know people don't like the association with military use of autonomous and semi-autonomous aircrafts.
